answer.sourceLine: This is Fuller’s own sentence, from chapter 4 of Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth (1969). Quote Investigator places it on pages 52–53 of that chapter and says it confirmed the wording against scans of the original text.

source.heading: The 1969 book it comes from

docMeta.dd: 1969 · Southern Illinois University Press, Carbondale — the edition Quote Investigator cites

source.excerpt: We have not been seeing our Spaceship Earth as an integrally-designed machine which to be persistently successful must be comprehended and serviced in total. Now there is one outstandingly important fact regarding Spaceship Earth, and that is that no instruction book came with it.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation of the line ↗ concludes that Fuller “deserves credit for the remark he wrote in 1969,” cites chapter 4 of Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth at quote pages 52–53, and states that it verified the passage against scans.

The book is catalogued at the Internet Archive as Operating manual for spaceship earth ↗ — Fuller, R. Buckminster, 1895–1983; Simon and Schuster, New York, 1969 (6th printing). That is a Simon and Schuster printing rather than the Southern Illinois University Press edition QI cites, so its pagination need not match. The copy is lending-restricted, so we did not read the page images ourselves.

The chapter attribution checks out independently: Wikipedia’s article on the book ↗ lists its eight chapters and gives “Spaceship Earth” as the fourth and “General systems theory” as the fifth — matching both QI’s chapter 4 and the “p. 58, Ch. 5, General Systems Theory” citation on Wikiquote’s page for the same book ↗. Neither of those pages carries this sentence itself, so neither is a second witness to the wording — only to where it sits.
source.excerptNote: Fuller presses the point in the same chapter: “In view of the infinite attention to all other details displayed by our ship, it must be taken as deliberate and purposeful that an instruction book was omitted.”

author.heading: About R. Buckminster Fuller
author.metaLine: 1895–1983 · American architect, systems theorist, inventor and futurist
author.bio: Fuller styled himself R. Buckminster Fuller and published more than thirty books arguing that design, not politics, would decide whether humanity managed to keep itself alive. He is best remembered for the geodesic dome and for a private vocabulary of coinages — Dymaxion, ephemeralization, synergetics — built to describe the planet as one engineered system. Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth (1969) is the short book that carried the idea furthest.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Fuller’s argument in the book is that the planet is a machine with no manual — and that the omission is the point, because it forces its passengers to work out how the thing runs. The sentence is the hinge of that argument rather than a stray aphorism.

The image travelled a long way from the book. Quote Investigator notes that others have written about the absence of an instruction manual quite independently, including a 1952 Ohio newspaper editorial about the Bible, Richard Dreyfuss in 1982, and William Nicholson’s play Shadowlands, so a reader who half-remembers “no instruction manual for life” is not necessarily remembering Fuller.
detailsBody: Fuller styled his name R. Buckminster Fuller in print, which is why his pages here carry that form rather than “Richard Buckminster Fuller Jr.”
context.pull: A machine with no manual, and the omission is deliberate.
